      "n": null,

      "verbatim": "The magnitude of change in oxidative stress biomarkers measured in our study ranges from 5 to 45 % after exercise with or without vitamin C administration, which is in general agreement with most of the relevant studies (reviewed in Braakhuis 2012; Fisher-Wellman and Bloomer 2009)."

    {

      "n": null,

      "verbatim": "The magnitude of changes in inflammation biomarkers in response to acute exercise with or without vitamin C administration ranges from 4 to 250 %, which is also in general agreement with most of the relevant studies (reviewed in Elkington et al. 2015; Walsh et al. 2011)."

    {
      "statistic": "vitamin C × species interaction",

      "n": 19,
      "n_counts": "biomarkers",
      "verbatim": "In contrast, as regards to the effects of vitamin C administration at rest, 10 significant interactions (in GSH, GSH/ GSSG, SOD, vitamin C, uric acid, bilirubin, TAC, CRP, IL-8 and IL-10) were observed out of the 19 biomarkers measured indicating that the rat poorly mimics human oxidative stress and inflammatory responses to vitamin C administration."

      "verbatim": "In agreement with this mechanistic work, we observed a greater than double increase in vitamin C plasma levels in humans compared to rats (92 vs. 41 %, respectively), suggesting impaired bioavailability of vitamin C in rats."

  "headline_index": 0,
  "what_the_study_did": "The study compared oxidative stress and inflammation responses between rats and humans to exercise and/or vitamin C administration.",
  "what_it_found": "Rats adequately mimic human responses to exercise but not to vitamin C administration. Vitamin C decreased oxidative stress in humans but induced an anti-inflammatory state in rats.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "The rat adequately mimics human responses to exercise in basic blood redox/inflammatory profile, yet this is not the case after vitamin C administration.",
      "topic": "Exercise vs Vitamin C"
    },
    {
      "quote": "The fact that only one exercise × species interaction (in catalase) was observed from the 19 biomarkers measured indicates that rats adequately mimic human oxidative stress and inflammatory responses to exercise.",
      "topic": "Exercise mimicry"
    },
    {
      "quote": "In contrast, as regards to the effects of vitamin C administration at rest, 10 significant interactions (in GSH, GSH/ GSSG, SOD, vitamin C, uric acid, bilirubin, TAC, CRP, IL-8 and IL-10) were observed out of the 19 biomarkers measured indicating that the rat poorly mimics human oxidative stress and inflammatory responses to vitamin C administration.",
      "topic": "Vitamin C mimicry"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Vitamin C decreased oxidative stress only in humans, whereas it decreased inflammation only in rats.",
      "topic": "Opposed effects"
    },
    {
      "quote": "We observed a greater than double increase in vitamin C plasma levels in humans compared to rats (92 vs. 41 %, respectively), suggesting impaired bioavailability of vitamin C in rats.",
      "topic": "Bioavailability difference"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Therefore, extrapolating data from rats to humans is not as straightforward as frequently assumed and clearly different stimuli can produce divergent results.",
      "topic": "Extrapolation caution"
